comparisons.peer_summary: Pursuant to Section 23A and 23B of the Federal Reserve Act and Regulation W, the Banks face quantitative and qualitative limits on credit extensions, asset purchases, and other transactions with nonbank affiliates, requiring such transactions to be on arm's length terms consistent with safety and soundness standards.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Bank of America disclose restrictions driven by U.S. banking safety and soundness standards, but they apply to different operational areas. Citi's disclosure (target) focuses on an accounting provision (ACL build) resulting from legal restrictions on holding unremittable corporate dividends, whereas Bank of America's candidate focuses on general regulatory limits (Section 23A/23B) on transactions with nonbank affiliates to ensure arm's length and safety standards.

sentences.text: Citi had an ACL build of $0.1 billion on other financial assets carried at amortized cost for the fourth quarter of 2024, primarily due to an increase in transfer risk associated with unremittable corporate dividends outside the U.S. being held on behalf of clients, driven by safety and soundness considerations under U.S. banking law.
Additionally, transactions between U.S. banks and their nonbank affiliates are required to be on arm's length terms and must be consistent with standards of safety and soundness.

comparisons.peer_summary: Federal law limits dividends paid by national banks, and regulators may prohibit dividends deemed unsafe or unsound given the bank's financial condition.

Citi links safety and soundness to a specific $0.1 billion ACL build due to unremittable dividends, while JPMorgan links the concept to regulators' authority to prohibit dividends if deemed an unsafe or unsound practice given the bank's financial condition.

sentences.text: Citi had an ACL build of $0.1 billion on other financial assets carried at amortized cost for the fourth quarter of 2024, primarily due to an increase in transfer risk associated with unremittable corporate dividends outside the U.S. being held on behalf of clients, driven by safety and soundness considerations under U.S. banking law.

The OCC and the Federal Reserve also have authority to prohibit or limit the payment of dividends of a bank subsidiary that they supervise if, in the banking regulator's opinion, payment of a dividend would constitute an unsafe or unsound practice in light of the financial condition of the bank.
